MINUTES
  Regular Meeting
  ALHAMBRA CITY COUNCIL
  Council Chambers, 111 South First Street
  July 27, 2026
  6:00 p.m.

ROLL CALL: At 6:06 p.m., on Monday, July 27, 2026, the Alhambra City Council met in the
Council Chambers of Alhambra City Hall.

PRESENT:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
ABSENT:  NONE

Officials Present: City Manager Binnquist, Assistant City Manager Garcia, City Attorney Montes,
Assistant City Clerk Lamb McCarthy, Director of Parks and Recreation Macias, Director of
Finance Lieu, Director of Community Development Ho, Associate Planner Vargas, Director of
Public Works and Utilities Ahlen, Chief of Fire Department Ragusa, Chief of Police Kennedy,
Director of Library Services LohGuan, Director of Human Resources Ko, Management Analyst
Alvarez

FLAG SALUTE:  Led by Mayor Maloney

LAND ACKNOWLEDGEMENT: We acknowledge that the land on which we are gathered is the
traditional, ancestral, and unceded territory of the Gabrielino/Tongva peoples. We seek to
prioritize respect for the historic culture and contemporary presence of the native peoples
throughout California, especially in the greater Los Angeles/Alhambra area. We come with
respect and gratitude for the Gabrielino/Tongva people who still consider themselves the
caretakers of this land. It is through their examples that we are reminded of our greater
responsibility to take care of Mother Earth and to take care of each other.

CEREMONIAL

1.  WELCOME TO SISTER CITY MUNICIPAL GOVERNMENT DELEGATION OF
  KIRISHIMA CITY, KAGOSHIMA PREFECTURE, JAPAN – F2M7-80

  Mayor MALONEY and the City Council presented a commemorative plaque and
  welcomed Mayor Shinichi NAKASHIGE and the delegation from the Municipal
  Government of Kirishima City during their visit to Alhambra in recognition of the enduring
  friendship and partnership between the sister cities.

  Congresswomen Judy CHU and Consulate General of Japan in Los Angeles, Murota
  KOSEI welcomed Mayor Shinichi Nakashige and the delegation from the Municipal
  Government and acknowledged the Alhambra City Councils efforts in this partnership.

  Mr. NAKASHIGE and Mr. MALONEY both signed a ceremonial certificate presented by
  Mr. Nakashige and the delegation presented Mr. Maloney with a traditional tin plaque from
  Kirishima City.

2.  CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE: JOSEPH INIGUEZ – F2M26-3

  1
7-27-26
   Mayor Maloney and the City Council presented a Certificate of Service plaque to Parks
  Supervisor Joseph Iniguez who retired after 31 years of faithful and loyal service to the
  Parks and Recreation Department and the City of Alhambra.

3.  CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE: NATALIA ROSALES – F2M22-3

  Mayor Maloney and the City Council presented a Certificate of Service certificate to
  recognize Natalia Rosales, who recently completed three terms on the Youth Commission,
  for her dedicated service to the City of Alhambra.

PUBLIC COMMENT FOR NON-AGENDIZED ITEMS (TIME LIMITATIONS: 3 MINUTES PER
SPEAKER, 30 MINUTES TOTAL)

1) Justin Love urged the City Council to review the current noise ordinance and noise vibration
  limits along the Main Street corridor, considering the area's mixed-use zoning. Mr. Love noted
  that he shares a common wall with a restaurant, and its air intake faces his living room window,
  which he is unable to open due to concerns related to noise and vibration.

2) Colin Campbell, representing Adapps Inc. and Mars Society – Pasadena Chapter, sought the
  City Councils support on joining an initiatives to move towards fusion power to help support
  clean water and building infrastructure. Mr. Campbell also submitted his comments via email.

3) Mary Hosokawa, acknowledged the concerts at the parks and requested a Trader Joes and
  Ross to come into the City.

4) Yuan Yin Li, via a Mandarin interpreter from the Language Network service, discussed a
  parking violation and the numerous attempts to pay the fine, as well as the difficulties
  experienced in obtaining reimbursement for the multiple payments made.

5) Christiopher Crespin and Hector Ornelas, representing the Alhambra Men’s Club, expressed
  concern regarding Almansor Park and the recent lack of attention it has been receiving for
  Golf players, considering the level of maintenance and care the park received in previous
  years.

6) “Public Toilet,” spoke in opposition of the Japanese military, referencing the capture of his
  grandmother several years ago.

PUBLIC HEARING

4.  PUBLIC HEARING TO ADOPT ORDINANCE O2M26-4869 APPROVING ZONING TEXT
  AMENDMENT AMD-26-07, AMENDING TITLE 23 (ZONING) OF THE ALHAMBRA
  MUNICIPAL CODE, AND ZONING MAP AMENDMENT AMD-26-05, AN AMENDMENT
  TO THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA OFFICIAL ZONING MAP; ADOPT RESOLUTION
  R2M26-23 APPROVING GENERAL PLAN TEXT AMENDMENT AMD-26-08,
  AMENDING THE GENERAL PLAN LAND USE ELEMENT, AND GENERAL PLAN MAP
  AMENDMENT AMD-26-06, AN AMENDMENT TO THE CITY OF ALHAMBRA
  GENERAL PLAN LAND USE MAP; AND ADOPT RESOLUTION R2M26-24
  APPROVING THE FOCUS AREA DESIGN GUIDELINES FOR WEST MAIN STREET,
  EAST MAIN STREET, AND VALLEY BOULEVARD; AND DETERMINE THIS ACTION
  IS EXEMPT FROM CEQA – F2M24-42, F2M26-37, O2M26-4869, R2M26-23, R2M26-24
  2
7-27-26
   Senior Planner, Megan WU presented a staff report and Jamie WILLIAMS of RRM Design
  Group delivered a presentation, which is on file in the City Clerk’s office. This was the time
  and place set by Notice No. N2M26-84 for the City Council to hold a public hearing to
  consider an application for Zoning Text Amendment AMD-26-07, Zoning Map Amendment
  AMD-26-05, General Plan Text Amendment AMD-26-08, and General Plan Map
  Amendment AMD-26-06. Zoning Text Amendment AMD-26-07, Zoning Map Amendment
  AMD-26-05, General Plan Text Amendment AMD-26-08, and General Plan Map
  Amendment AMD-26-06 were City-initiated applications to update the City’s existing
  objective design standards in Title 23 (Zoning) of the Alhambra Municipal Code, as well
  as eliminate the West Main Corridor Master Plan Overlay District Zoning classification and
  the corresponding Downtown Specific Plan Overlay General Plan Land Use designation,
  to accommodate adoption of new focus-area design guidelines. The proposed
  amendments were intended to facilitate and encourage quality design in the City, and
  would also ensure City documents reflect internal consistency in their references to
  General Plan Land Use designations and Zoning classifications. Additionally, updates
  were proposed to rectify prior mapping errors for two (2) existing parcels at APN 5364-
  018-019 and 5364-018-020.

  The City’s adopted 2021-2029 Housing Element included programs to establish design
  guidelines and city-wide objective design standards. Additionally, the City Council’s
  Strategic Plan identified development of design guidelines for multi-family residential,
  commercial, and mixed-use developments to further the goal of improving housing
  opportunities in the City. While design guidelines have provided recommendations that
  encourage high-quality architecture and reinforce the City’s desired community character,
  objective design standards are required under various State housing laws to ensure
  qualifying development projects are reviewed and approved using measurable, objective
  criteria, rather than subjective or discretionary judgment. The proposed design guidelines
  and design standards pertained to regulating and guiding the architecture and design of
  buildings and did not propose to change any physical development standards such as
  density, setbacks, height, or parking.

  On May 18, 2026, the Planning Commission conducted a duly noticed public hearing to
  consider the proposed Zoning Text Amendment, Zoning Map Amendment, General Plan
  Text Amendment, and General Plan Map Amendment. Following the public hearing, the
  Planning Commission unanimously adopted Resolution No. 26-07 recommending that the
  City Council approve the proposed amendments. Once adopted by the City Council, the
  updates to the objective design standards would go into effect 40 days after final approval
  and adoption of the Ordinance, and these standards would be applied to new projects
  going forward. The newly adopted design guidelines would become effective upon the
  effective date of the Ordinance adopting the updated objective design standards and
  eliminating the West Main Street Corridor Master Plan area. While the new standards and
  design guidelines would start being implemented for new projects later this year, the
  timeline of when the community would start seeing the fruition of these new standards and
  guidelines in future development projects could be several years.

  Finally, the City reviewed the environmental impacts of the proposed Ordinance and City
  Council Resolutions under the California Environmental Quality Act (Public Resources
  Code §§ 21000, et seq. “CEQA”) and the regulations promulgated thereunder (14 Cal.
  Code of Regs. §§ 15000, et seq., the “CEQA Guidelines”). This Ordinance and City
  Council Resolutions were not subject to further review environmental review because: (1)
  3
7-27-26
   it would not result in a direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect physical change in the
  environment (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15060(c)(2); (2) there was no possibility that this
  Ordinance or City Council Resolutions would have a significant effect on the environment
  (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15061(b)(3)); and (3) the Ordinance and City Council Resolutions,
  by itself, did not constitute a “project” as defined in section 21065 of the Public Resources
  Code and the CEQA Guidelines (14 Cal. Code Regs. § 15378). It could be seen with
  certainty that there was no possibility that this Ordinance and City Council Resolutions
  could have a significant effect on the environment.

  Open Public Hearing:  Mayor Maloney opened the public hearing.

  Public Comment:

  1) Lewis McCammon, spoke in favor of the zoning amendment but requested that the
  information be provided in color for clearer visual understanding.

  Public Comment received via email, and on file in the City Clerk’s office:  Marisol
  Grier requested consideration of the East Main Corridor.

  Close Public Hearing:  After receiving public comment, Mayor Maloney closed the
  public hearing.

  Discussion:  Vice Mayor Andrade-Stadler spoke in support of the flexible zoning
  amendment and the design guidelines shaping a Spanish/Mission style downtown.

  Councilmember WANG received clarification on state law mandates, requiring objective
  design standards and local policy incorporating design guidelines.

  Council Member MAZA received clarification on the design guidelines being reviewed by
  the Designer View Board Committee to reassure compliance.

  Council Member LEE spoke in support of the proposed zoning amendment and provided
  comments on maintaining the mission style design standard for the downtown area, while
  allowing businesses flexibility in designing their storefronts.

  Mayor MALONEY proposed updating the language to replace vegetation and specify that
  native plant species should be used and non-native plant species may be used in the rare
  circumstances.

  Action Taken:  City Council took the following actions:

  1) Introduced and give first reading by title only, waiving further reading to the following
  ordinance entitled:

  Ordinance No. O2M26-4869: An Ordinance of the City Council of the City of Alhambra
  Adopting Zoning Text Amendment AMD-26-07, Amending Title 23 (Zoning) of the
  Alhambra Municipal Code to Update the City-Wide Objective Design Standards and
  Eliminate the West Main Corridor Master Plan Overlay District, and Zoning Map
  Amendment AMD-26-05, an Amendment to the City of Alhambra Official Zoning Map
  including language to replace vegetation and specify native plant species should be
  utilized, with non-native plant species permitted only in rare circumstances

  4
7-27-26
   which ordinance would return for a second reading and adoption at the next City
  Council meeting on August 24, 2026;

  2) Adopted the following Resolution entitled:

  Resolution No. R2M26-23: A Resolution of the City Council of the City of Alhambra,
  California Approving General Plan Text Amendment AMD-26-08, an Amendment to the
  City of Alhambra General Plan Land Use Element, and General Plan Map Amendment
  AMD-26-06, an Amendment to the City of Alhambra General Plan Land Use Map

  3) Adopted the following Resolution entitled:

  Resolution No. R2M26-24: A Resolution of the City Council of the City of Alhambra,
  California approving focus area design guidelines, for West Main Street, East Main Street,
  and Valley Boulevard.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded: LEE
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

PRESENTATIONS

5.  CITYWIDE STREETLIGHTING MASTER PLAN - F2M25-30

  Director of Public Works, Dennis AHLEN presented the 2026 Strategic Plan, reaffirming
  Goal One: Enhance Public Safety. One of goal’s objectives is the development of a
  Citywide Streetlighting Master Plan. Brian GATES, of Evari Consulting, delivered a
  presentation. On July 28, 2025, City Council approved an award of contract C2M25-36 to
  Evari Consulting, Inc. to evaluate the lighting conditions, and to create a Master Plan for
  replacement and/or conversion. During the study, Evari Consulting conducted an
  inventory of all city owned street light; took illuminance readings from every lane mile of
  City roadway; assessed the current age and conditions of the system, and developed a
  citywide lighting model. A five-year and ten-year capital improvement plan was prepared
  detailing the costs and options for implementation. Also, the Plan provided for the
  conversion of 4,883 existing light fixtures to LED lighting, which work could be performed
  by a combination of staff and contracted services. The plan also detailed solar lighting
  options and recommended series circuit S-142 bounded by Granada Avenue, Valley
  Boulevard, Almansor Street and Shorb Street as a candidate for a pilot solar project. If
  approved, staff would bring back an RFP for a pilot solar streetlight project to replace
  circuit S-142 with solar lighting. Dan Sanders, with Klein and Associates, was present to
  provide additional clarification.

  Public Comment:  Lewis McCammon, via Zoom, emphasized the importance of
  prioritizing circuits where lights are currently going out, and was pleased to see the
  potential for solar lighting to replace hardwired fixtures.

  Public Comment received via email and on file in the City Clerk’s office:  Kathy
  Lau wrote regarding streetlight failures on the 2500 block of Stranahan Drive.

  Discussion: Councilmember LEE received clarification on the program cost of solar
  lighting compared to our current conventional lighting systems, noting a 60 percent cost
  5
7-27-26
   reduction for solar lighting, with batteries needing replacement approximately every seven
  years and panels approximately every twenty years.

  Councilmember MAZA emphasized the preference for LED lighting over warm color tones.

  Councilmember WANG examined parallel circuits and analyzed the current distribution
  and lighting throughout the city, emphasizing the importance of assessing the area around
  her residential home, where a complete section experiences power outages whenever
  there are issues with a single light pole, highlighting the safety concerns in darker regions
  with consistent power outages. Councilmember WANG urged staff to prioritize District 4
  and 5 and move towards solar lighting or potential pilot an area within these districts.

  Vice Mayor ANDRADE-STADLER commented on consistent power outages affecting light
  poles, which can last on average from one week to a month, as well as safety concerns in
  darker residential areas.

  Councilmember WANG urged staff to prioritize District 4 and 5 and move towards solar
  lighting across the City and potential pilot an area within these districts.

  City Manager BINNQUIST noted if the City Council decides to implement solar lighting
  throughout the city, there will be an impact on the current budget, as this was not
  accounted for in the original financial plan. Therefore, staff recommended starting with a
  pilot program to evaluate its effectiveness before considering a broader transition to solar
  lighting in future discussions.

  Mayor MALONEY agreed with the City Council's comments and concerns and
  acknowledged the receipt and file of this report, noting for staff to include this item on the
  agenda for future discussions regarding the pilot program and potentially additional solar
  lighting.

  Action Taken:  Council received and filed the Citywide Streetlighting Master Plan
  and directed staff to proceed with a solar pilot project as identified in the Master Plan.

  Vote:  Moved:  MALONEY  Seconded: ANDRADE-STADLER
  Ayes:  LEE, MAZA, WANG, ANDRADE-STADLER, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

CONSENT AGENDA (Item Nos. 6 – 21): (TIME LIMITATIONS: 5 MINUTES PER SPEAKER
FOR ONE ITEM, 10 MINUTES PER SPEAKER FOR 2+ ITEMS)

All items listed under the Consent Agenda, with the exception of Item No. 19, was considered by the
City Council to be routine and were enacted by one motion.

6.  2026 STRATEGIC PLAN UPDATE – F2M26-27

  On April 13, 2026, the City Council approved the 2026 Strategic Plan following two special
  City Council meetings that were conducted to review and update the goals and objectives
  that were previously established in the 2025 Strategic Plan. The 2026 Strategic Plan
  contained six Goals: Goal 1: Enhance Public Safety; Goal 2: Improve Infrastructure and
  Mobility; Goal 3: Create a Strong Financial Base and Strong Economic Base (Economic
  6
7-27-26
   Development); Goal 4: Enhance Transparency and Open Governance; Goal 5: Promote
  Sustainability; and, Goal 6: Improve Housing Opportunities. Staff would continue to
  present quarterly updates to the Council and would diligently work through Strategic Plan
  goals and individual items to enable important progress.

  Public Comment:  “Public Toilet”, highlighting the need for additional public restrooms,
  an evaluation of traffic light sensors, and increased enforcement of e-bike regulations.
  Additionally, addressed Goal 6, expressing concern that affordable housing remains a low
  priority for the City and emphasizing the city's responsibility to facilitate the creation of
  more affordable housing units.

  Discussion:  Councilmember LEE noted her consistent opposition towards the
  zoning update within the Strategic Plan Update.

  Action Taken:  City Council received and file dthe 2026 Strategic Plan update.

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

7.  AWARD OF CONTRACT: TECHNICAL AND PROJECT MANAGEMENT SERVICES
  FOR PRIORITY PEDESTRIAN IMPROVEMENTS - F2M25-62, C2M26-45, M2M26-120

  On March 11, 2024, the City Council adopted the City’s Bicycle and Pedestrian
  Improvement Plan (“Walk, Bike, Move Alhambra!”), which established a vision for biking
  and pedestrian infrastructure and facilitated further planning and funding support for the
  implementation of the City’s multi-modal transportation goals. The City received a Funding
  Agreement in the amount of $14,387,027.50 in Measure R funds for the Citywide Priority
  Pedestrian Improvement Project which would cover the design, engineering, and
  construction associated with improving the eight priority pedestrian locations identified in
  the City’s Plan. On May 11, 2026 the City awarded a contract for the design engineering
  services of the Project’s Phase 1 PS&E and Phase 2 Preliminary Engineering to AYCE
  Consulting Engineers, Inc. Staff recommended awarding a Professional Services
  Agreement to Transtech Engineers Inc. for technical and project management services
  associated with the pedestrian improvement project, with a not-to-exceed budget of
  $74,650, to support the completion of the project. Transtech Engineers Inc. has served as
  the City’s Transportation Engineer under the current Public Works Department contract
  and has provided assistance with special projects as needed. Pursuant to Section 3, “City
  Engineering Services,” Item E, “Capital Projects,” of the contract, Transtech was
  authorized to provide engineering services for capital projects upon receiving specific and
  separate authorization from the City. Due to the extensive nature of the work associated
  with this project it was determined that a separate agreement is appropriate.

  Public Comment:  “Public Toilet,” expressed the need for additional public restrooms,
  as facilities at public parks and other locations, such as Almansor Park, close at 9:00 p.m

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council awarded a contract to Transtech Engineers Inc.,
  subject to final language approval by the City Manager and City Attorney, in the amount

  7
7-27-26
   of $74,650.00 for technical and project management services for the City’s Priority
  Pedestrian Improvements under the Alhambra Bicycle and Pedestrian Improvement Plan.
  (M2M26-120)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

8.  APPROPRIATION FROM THE EQUIPMENT FUND RESERVE FOR THE PURCHASE
  OF ONE POLICE PATROL MOTORCYCLE FOR THE ALHAMBRA POLICE
  DEPARTMENT – F2M26-17, M2M26-121

  On March 20, 2026, Patrol Motorcycle Unit 538 was struck by another vehicle while
  conducting a traffic stop, resulting in extensive damage. Following inspection, the City’s
  insurance adjuster determined the motorcycle was a total loss. The California Joint
  Powers Insurance Authority (JPIA) issued an insurance settlement to the City in the
  amount of $33,246.44 due to current market conditions and the increased costs for a
  replacement patrol motorcycle, the insurance settlement was insufficient to cover the full
  replacement cost. The estimated purchase price of a replacement motorcycle was
  $46,555.09, resulting in a funding shortfall of $13,308.65. Staff requested an appropriation
  in the amount of $13,308.65 from the Equipment Fund Reserves to fully fund the
  replacement purchase.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council approved an appropriation of $13,308.65 from the
  Equipment Fund Reserve for the purchase of one police patrol motorcycle; directed the
  Finance Director to transfer insurance settlement revenues in the amount of $32,246.44
  to complete the purchase; and, directed staff to undertake the steps necessary to finalize
  the Council’s action. (M2M26-121)

  Vote:  Moved:  ANDRADE-STADLER  Seconded:  WANG
  Ayes:  LEE, ANDRADE-STADLER, WANG, MAZA, MALONEY
  Noes:  NONE
  Absent:  NONE

9.  APPROVAL OF SECOND CONTRACT AMENDMENT WITH YUNEX, LLC FOR FY
  2025-2026 – F2M25-31, C2M25-41, M2M26-122

  On September 22, 2025, the City Council awarded a contract to YUNEX LLC in the amount
  of $240,000.00 for Traffic Signal and Street Lighting Maintenance Services. On March 23,
  2026, the City Council approved an amendment in the amount of $120,000.00 for
  additional property damage and repairs. Since then, the City has received all invoices and
  experienced an increase in emergency response and additional property damage and
  repairs, resulting in the contract fully exhausted by the April 2026 billing. Staff requested
  additional appropriations in the amount of $40,000.00 for the services provided under the
  2025-2026 Fiscal year.

  Discussion:  None.

7-27-26

14.  RATIFY THE ACCEPTANCE OF GRANT FUNDS FROM CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY
  PATROL CANNABIS TAX FUND PROGRAM – F2M26-18, R2M26-25, M2M26-124

  The goal of the California Highway Patrol (CHP) grant was to educate the public about the
  dangers of impaired driving, enforce laws related to impaired driving on the road, and
  enhance the effectiveness of the Alhambra Police Department (APD) through training and
  the development of new strategies. The APD planned to utilize funding in Fiscal Year
  2026-27 to conduct saturation patrol operations focused on driving under the influence
  (DUI), targeting alcohol, other drugs, and cannabis products. The funding would cover the
  purchase of one fully outfitted, marked police motorcycle for use during DUI operations. It
  would also cover personnel expenses for patrol officers attending DUI-related training.
  10
7-27-26
   Due to summer recess, the City Manager accepted this grant; therefore, staff requested
  the City Council ratify the acceptance and directed the City Clerk to send a copy of the
  resolution to CHP.

  Discussion:  None.

  Action Taken:  City Council ratified the acceptance of the California Highway Patrol
  (CHP) Cannabis Tax Fund Grant Program funds in the amount of $299,556.40; Adopt
  Resolution No. R2M26-25 entitled: A Resolution of the City Council of the City of
  Alhambra, California, ratifying the acceptance of funds from Cannabis Tax Fund Grant
  Program; appropriate $299,556.40 in revenue and expenditure funds in the 2026-27 Fiscal

21.  SECOND READING OF AN ORDINANCE PROVIDING FOR A GENERAL MUNICIPAL
  ELECTION IN SAID CITY TO BE HELD ON NOVEMBER 3, 2026, PROVIDING FOR

  15
7-27-26
   THE CONSOLIDATION OF THE GENERAL MUNICIPAL ELECTION WITH THE
  STATEWIDE GENERAL ELECTION; SAID ELECTION BEING HELD FOR A BALLOT
  MEASURE TO AMEND ALHAMBRA MUNICIPAL CODE CHAPTER 5.70
  (“TRANSIENT OCCUPANCY TAX”) – F2M26-33, O2M26-4865

  Alhambra has provided a variety of essential municipal services, including Fire, Police,
  Emergency 911, youth and senior services, library, parks, public works and utilities. In
  recent years, the City’s ability to maintain these services has become more difficult with
  service costs increasing including costs from impacts to infrastructure and public safety
  from short-term vacation rentals in residential neighborhoods. Short-term vacation rentals
  have impacted local services and infrastructure just as traditional hotels; however, short-
  term rentals currently in Alhambra have not been paying the same transient occupancy
  tax imposed on traditional hotels. For the 2026-27 Fiscal Year Budget, the City’s finances
  showed a net zero unassigned General Fund Balance, meaning there have been no
  additional or surplus funds available to address a host of priorities including facility
  upgrades, reserve contributions, capital and equipment repair and replacement, and
  unfunded liability. The City must identify and secure funding streams, if adopted by
  Alhambra voters, which ensure visitor-related impacts would be funded by visitors and not
  residents. The City of Alhambra aims to preserve Alhambra’s quality of life, including well-
  maintained streets, quality of local parks, safe and clean neighborhoods, and rapid 911
  response. A local Transient Occupancy Tax (TOT) for short-term vacation rentals for stays
  up to 30 days at the same rate (12% of the rent charged by an operator of a hotel or motel)
  as specified under the City’s existing TOT under the Alhambra Municipal Code Chapter
  5.70 would help support the services the Alhambra community have designated as
  important at levels consistent with the community’s priorities. Calling the election requires
  adoption of an ordinance. The proposed ordinance would do the following: Set forth City
  Council approval of a TOT of 12% for short-term vacation rentals for stays up to 30 days,
  subject to Alhambra voter approval; Call a general municipal election on November 3,
  2026, for the purpose of submitting the Ballot Measure for consideration of the qualified
  electors of the City, modernizing the definitions of “transients” and “hotel” in the TOT
  Ordinance, while not changing the TOT rate of 12%, and that ballot measure would be
  presented as an amendment to a general tax imposed for general governmental purposes,
  with revenue from the tax to be placed in the City’s general fund to pay for any general
  governmental purpose; Direct the City Attorney to prepare the measure summary per
  Elections Code 9280; and, Sets out time frames and deadlines for submittal of ballot
  arguments and rebuttals.

  Public Comment:  Lewis MCCAMMON discussed the transient occupancy tax that
  would be present in the November 2026 Election for resident to vote.

  Discussion:  None

  Action Taken:  City Council, by one motion, took the following actions:

  1.  Found that the proposed action is not subject to the California Environmental
  Quality Act (“CEQA”) pursuant to Public Resources Code Section 21080(b)(8), and
  California Code of Regulations Section 15378(b)(5) because it relates to organizational or
  administrative activities of the City, it leads to the establishment of funding City services
  within existing service areas, and will not result in direct or indirect physical changes to
  the environment.
